title: Time Complexity
body:
How the running time of an [[Algorithm]] grows as the input grows. Not seconds: seconds
depend on the machine, the compiler, and what else is running. Time complexity counts
*operations* as a function of input size $n$, then throws away everything that stops
mattering when $n$ gets big. See [[Asymptotic Analysis]] for the machinery behind the
throwing away.

## Big O

$O(f(n))$ is an upper bound: the algorithm takes *at most* on the order of $f(n)$ steps.
Two rules do almost all the work:

1. **Drop constants.** $3n$ and $n$ are both $O(n)$. Doubling the machine speed does not
   change the shape of the curve.
2. **Drop lower-order terms.** $n^2 + n + 500$ is $O(n^2)$, because once $n$ is large the
   $n^2$ term buries the rest.

There are companions you will see less often: $\Omega$ is a lower bound and $\Theta$ is
both at once (a tight bound). Courses say "big O" and usually mean $\Theta$.

## The ladder

| Class | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $O(1)$ | constant | [[Array]] index, [[Hashing\|hash]] lookup (average), pushing to a [[Stack]] |
| $O(\log n)$ | logarithmic | binary search, [[Binary Search Tree]] search when balanced |
| $O(n)$ | linear | scanning a [[Linked List]], finding the max of an unsorted array |
| $O(n \log n)$ | linearithmic | [[Merge Sort]], [[Quick Sort]] average, heapsort |
| $O(n^2)$ | quadratic | [[Bubble Sort]], [[Insertion Sort]], comparing every pair |
| $O(2^n)$ | exponential | subsets, brute-force [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] |
| $O(n!)$ | factorial | every ordering, brute-force travelling salesman |

Each step down that table is a different world. An $O(n^2)$ algorithm on a million items is
$10^{12}$ operations; the $O(n \log n)$ version is about $2 \times 10^7$. That is the gap
between "overnight" and "before you finish reading this line".

## Counting it

Read the loops.

```java
// O(n): one pass
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += a[i]; }

// O(n^2): a pass inside a pass
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
        if (a[i] == a[j]) count++;

// O(log n): the problem halves every iteration
while (lo <= hi) {
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == key) return mid;
    else if (a[mid] < key) lo = mid + 1;
    else hi = mid - 1;
}
```

Sequential blocks add ($O(n) + O(n) = O(n)$), nested blocks multiply, and anything that
repeatedly halves the input is a logarithm.

## Best, average, worst

Three different questions, and the answer often differs.

- **Worst case** is the guarantee, and it is what "the complexity of X" means by default.
- **Average case** assumes typical input. [[Quick Sort]] lives here: $O(n \log n)$ average,
  $O(n^2)$ worst.
- **Best case** is mostly trivia, with one exception: [[Insertion Sort]] is $O(n)$ on
  nearly-sorted data, which is why real library sorts fall back to it on small ranges.

**Amortised** is a fourth thing and not the same as average. A [[Dynamic Arrays|dynamic array]]
append is $O(n)$ on the resize and $O(1)$ the rest of the time, and the resizes are rare enough
that the cost *per operation over a long run* is $O(1)$.

## Space too

The same notation applies to memory. [[Merge Sort]] is $O(n \log n)$ time but $O(n)$ extra
space; [[Quick Sort]] sorts in place. When the choice between two structures looks like a
tie on time, it is usually being decided on space: [[Adjacency Matrix]] at $O(V^2)$ versus
[[Adjacency List]] at $O(V + E)$ is exactly that trade.
